from_notes: Removed by | President only (same grounds and SC-inquiry procedure as NHRC)

from_notes: Consultation | Sitting HC Judge or District Judge appointed only after consulting the Chief Justice of the HC concerned
x: A sitting HC Judge or sitting District Judge can be appointed to an SHRC only after consulting the Chief Justice of the High Court of the State concerned.

from_notes: Appointed by | Governor
x: The SHRC Chairperson and members are appointed by the Governor on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Chief Minister.

from_notes: Acting Chairperson | Governor authorises a member in a vacancy
x: If the SHRC Chairperson's office falls vacant, the Governor may authorise one of the members to act as Chairperson.

from_notes: Annual report | To the State Government → laid before the State Legislature with a memorandum of action taken
x: The SHRC submits its annual or special reports to the State Government, which lays them before the State Legislature with a memorandum of action taken.

from_notes: Selection committee (Sec. 22) | Chief Minister (head), Speaker, State Home Minister, LoP in the Assembly; + Chairman and LoP of the Council where bicameral
x: Under Section 22, the committee recommending SHRC appointments is headed by the Chief Minister; the Governor appoints on its recommendation.
The President is the constitutional (nominal) head of India; the Prime Minister is the real executive head. Moved to the President row.
The NHRC can intervene in court proceedings only with the court's approval, so 'without the court's approval' is not a function. Inquiries (suo motu or on petition) and research are functions.
dispute: Printed key: option 2 (intervene without court approval). Strictly: the jail-visit option is also inaccurate, because the power covers jails under the State Government too, not 'Central Government only' (PHRA s.12(c); general knowledge, not checked).

x: In Youth Bar Association of India v Union of India (2016) the SC directed that FIR copies, except in sensitive cases, be uploaded on the police or State website within 24 hours of registration.

from_notes: Powers: like the NHRC – inquires suo motu, visits jails, reviews safeguards; can only recommend compensation to the Government; cannot punish.
x: An SHRC can inquire suo motu, visit jails and review safeguards, but it cannot punish violators; it only recommends.

from_notes: 13 | Powers of a civil court (CPC 1908) in inquiries; deemed civil court for offences under IPC 175, 178, 179, 180, 228
x: When an offence under IPC sections 175, 178, 179, 180 or 228 is committed before it, the Commission is deemed a civil court (Sec. 13 PHRA) and may forward the case to a Magistrate.
source: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Part 2 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02) p.228; app notes (old-notes.txt) 2:125 sub 3

from_notes: Powers: like the NHRC – inquires suo motu, visits jails, reviews safeguards; can only recommend compensation to the Government; cannot punish.
x: After an inquiry, an SHRC may only recommend that the State Government or authority pay compensation or damages; it cannot order payment itself.

from_notes: Watchdog of rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity – rights like education are not listed in the PHRA definition.
x: The PHRA defines human rights as rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity, so education is not listed in the Commission's purview.
source: Laxmikanth 8th ed. Part 2 (src/polity/laxmikanth-indian-polity-02) p.226; Rocket Polity (src/polity/rocket-polity-01) p.68

from_notes: Jurisdiction: only State List and Concurrent List subjects (not State List alone); does not inquire into a case the NHRC is probing.

Under Section 82 of the AP Reorganisation Act 2014, the employees of State PSUs are distributed between the two States as the concerned PSU's management decides. A bifurcation question, moved.

from_notes: Human Rights Courts (Sec. 30): a Court of Session in every district (State Govt + HC Chief Justice's concurrence); Special Public Prosecutor (Sec. 31) – advocate of 7 years.
x: Under Section 30 of the PHRA, the State Government, with the HC Chief Justice's concurrence, specifies a Court of Session in each district as a Human Rights Court. Collectorates, panchayats and gram sabhas are not courts.
Under the AP Lokayukta Act 1983 (as amended), the Lokayukta must be a retired Chief Justice or a Judge of a High Court, so option 2 is the best fit. Moved to the Lokayukta row.

from_notes: NHRC = statutory body, not constitutional, set up under the Protection of Human Rights Act (PHRA), 1993 passed by Parliament – not by an executive order of the President.
x: A is true: the NHRC inquires into violations or negligence by public servants. R is false: it derives its authority from the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, a law of Parliament, not an executive order.

Statement 1 is wrong: in judicial custody the accused is lodged in jail under the magistrate's custody, not in the police station. Statement 2 is right: police cannot interrogate the accused without the court's approval.

from_notes: Parole/furlough: not an absolute right – even a sufficient case does not make parole a matter of right; each State has its own Prisoners Release on Parole Rules (UPSC 2021).
x: Parole is not a matter of right even when a case is made out; it is a concession. State Governments have their own Prisoners Release on Parole Rules, so 2 only.

from_notes: UPSC 2023: Statement I (States manage prisons) and Statement II (1894 Act kept prisons with Provincial Governments) are both correct, and II explains I (widely given key).
x: Prisons are a State subject (State List Entry 4), so States run them with their own rules; the Prisons Act 1894 placed prisons under the Provincial (now State) Governments, which explains Statement I.
source: web search results (testbook, vajiramandravi: UPSC 2023 key a); app notes 2:127 sub 3
